Since his discovery of writing some seven years ago Thad'ja Songcatcher's life had both been exciting and exasperating; He had braved the raging storms and convinced the Flora to join his brethren at the tree of life, affording them the chance to learn much from the strange, tall, plant like people and the time to study their great pattern at his leisure. Sadly the Flora had grown disinterested in their proliferation of the pattern within months of their arrival at the tree of life leaving he and his brothers to study alone. These efforts too proved fruitless as the pattern was revealed to be little more than a trick of the God of chance following the arrival of a young Med'ja possessing an unknown power.

While his brothers had busied themselves with study of their new guest Thad'ja had attended to more pressing matters, namely the establishment of a school in the Gove of Hom to ensure that future generations of his kind would share the benefit of the brotherhoods script. For these efforts Thad'ja was rewarded, the inquisitive tribe accepting his offer and taking to the study with a fervour to rival his brothers at the Great Tree. The glow of this success was sadly short-lived as his now celebrity status within the Brotherhood of Umbralocht required him to spend greater and greater time away from his students. In the end it was decided that Thad'ja Songcatcher would preside over the entirety of the Brotherhood's works becoming both the Great Tree's first librarian and the Cult's unofficial leader, the first they had had in generations.

So it was that Songcatcher found himself in the process of developing a system to catalogue the vast works of the Brotherhood when the drums of war began to beat beneath the Great Tree, the Flora having become the target of an approaching army from the north. The army that arrived of course was not the one that they had expected, the Chlora having been pacified before even setting foot within the Southern Forest. Instead the Great Tree, the Flora and the soldiers sent to defend them found themselves under assault by strange, floating spheres which had somehow in their own right angered Hom, their God who had until now had been seen to interfere little in the day to day lives of his children.

With Hom's awakening and the smiting of their foe, he bestowed upon the brotherhood a gift in the form of an enchanted staff which not only would summon a horde of insects for the user to command but could also reveal the nature of objects it came into contact with. Much to his vexation the Brotherhood decided that the responsibility of the staff should fall to him granting Thad'ja Songcatcher not only the responsibility to lead and organise but to defend the tree and reveal the nature of any unknowns the brotherhood may come across. It was all too much for one Med'ja to bear. His first action as holder of the staff was determine what exactly had attacked the tree and its residents which once again lead to disappointment.

The Orbs left in the God's wake had surprisingly little to reveal; thought made of an exceeding strong metal they were merely hollow puppets controlled by the God of Order himself and had simply become lifeless at his departure. Serving little more than to pollute the landscape of the forest the soldiers had claimed several as spoils of war while the rest were left to be claimed by the forest and decay for the Med'ja lacked the technique and tools to work with such a material and the Shamans were simply disinterested.

AS life returned to normal for the Cult of Umbralocht the powers of the staff of Hom fell into disuse until one day, some 5 years after its appearance they received word from the Grove of Hom that a bizarre creature had been found lurking within their brewery....

God this fallacy again?

One especially robust fallacy is the belief that machines on net balance create unemployment. Destroyed a thousand times, it has risen a thousand times out of its own ashes as hardy and vigorous as ever. This time, the government is not the sole coercive agent. The Luddite rebellion in early 19th-century England is the prime example.

Labor unions have succeeded in restricting automation and other labor-saving improvements in many cases. The half-truth of the fallacy is evident here. Jobs are destroyed for particular groups and in the short term. Overall, the wealth created by using the labor-saving devices and practices generates far more jobs than are lost directly.

Arkwright invented his cotton-spinning machinery in 1760. The use of it was opposed on the ground that it threatened the livelihood of the workers, and the opposition had to be put down by force. 27 years later, there were over 40 times as many people working in the industry.

What happens when jobs are destroyed by a new machine? The employer will use his savings in one or more of three ways:

(1) to expand his operations by buying more machines;

(2) to invest the extra profits in some other industry; or

(3) spend the extra profits on his own consumption.

The direct effect of this spending will be to create as many jobs as were destroyed. The overall net effect to the economy is to create wealth and even more jobs. We must remember that the short-term local effect is to destroy jobs. In some cases where this effect is major, special relief measures through charities and non-profits might be taken, but blocking the progress leads to stagnation and poverty.
